content: Phantom limb pain (PLP) is a type of pain that occurs in the area of a missing limb following amputation. This pain can be severe, persistent, and disabling. Various medications have been studied to treat PLP, but there is still no clear consensus on the most effective pharmacologic treatment. In this updated review, researchers aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of different pharmacologic interventions for PLP. They included randomized and quasi-randomized trials that compared medications to placebo, other active treatments, or no treatment. The outcomes assessed included changes in pain intensity, function, sleep, mood, quality of life, adverse events, treatment satisfaction, and study withdrawals. The review included 14 studies with a total of 269 participants. Among these, 10 studies were considered to have a low risk of bias, while 4 had an unclear risk of bias. A new drug class, botulinum neurotoxins (BoNTs), specifically botulinum toxin A (BoNT/A), was added to the list of medications reviewed. The primary outcome of interest was the change in pain intensity, while secondary outcomes such as sleep, mood, and quality of life were less frequently reported. The findings for BoNT/A showed that it did not reduce phantom limb pain intensity over six months when compared to lidocaine/methylprednisolone. Morphine, both oral and intravenous, was effective in reducing pain intensity in the short term compared to placebo. However, it was associated with several adverse effects, including constipation, sedation, tiredness, dizziness, sweating, difficulty urinating, vertigo, itching, and respiratory issues. N-methyl D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonists, such as ketamine and dextromethorphan, demonstrated analgesic effects. Ketamine, when compared to placebo or calcitonin, showed pain relief but was associated with more severe adverse effects, including loss of consciousness, sedation, hallucinations, impaired hearing and balance, and feelings of intoxication. Memantine, another NMDA receptor antagonist, did not show effectiveness for PLP. Gabapentin showed mixed results for pain relief, but when the data were combined, it appeared to favor the treatment group over placebo. However, gabapentin did not improve function, mood, or sleep quality. Adverse effects of gabapentin included drowsiness, dizziness, headache, and nausea. Amitriptyline, compared to benztropine mesylate, was not effective for PLP. The most common side effects of amitriptyline were dry mouth and dizziness. The results for calcitonin and local anesthetics were inconsistent. Calcitonin was associated with side effects such as headache, vertigo, drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, and hot and cold flushes. Most of the studies included in the review were limited by small sample sizes, which makes it difficult to draw definitive conclusions. The authors concluded that the evidence for the effectiveness of BoNT/A, opioids, NMDA receptor antagonists, anticonvulsants, antidepressants, calcitonins, and local anesthetics in treating PLP remains inconclusive. While morphine, gabapentin, and ketamine showed some short-term benefits, their long-term efficacy and safety are unclear. Medications like memantine and amitriptyline may not be effective for PLP. Further research with larger, more rigorous randomized controlled trials is needed to determine which medications are most effective for clinical use.
